title: Pharaoh had a throne.
paragraphs:
Pharaoh had a throne.
He had an army.
He had absolute power over Egypt.
And one day, he gave an order that would echo through history.
Every Hebrew baby boy must die.

Not on a battlefield.
Not in war.
But at birth.

Quietly. Systematically.
Before anyone could even know their name.

Pharaoh believed something dangerous was happening. The Hebrew people were multiplying and growing strong (Exodus 1:7–10). Fear took hold of his heart, and fear often turns into oppression when power is involved.
So he devised a cruel solution.
He summoned two women whose profession placed them at the very beginning of life.
Midwives.
Their names were Shiphrah and Puah.
In Pharaoh’s mind, this was the perfect strategy. No rebellion. No public spectacle. Just a quiet command carried out in hidden rooms.
When a Hebrew woman gives birth, he told them, if the child is a boy, kill him.

No one would notice.
No one would question it.
Or so he thought.
But Pharaoh underestimated something far stronger than his authority.
The fear of God.
Scripture says something simple, yet incredibly powerful:

“But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live.”
— Exodus 1:17
Two women.
One command from the most powerful ruler in the land.
And they refused.
Think about the courage this required.
Pharaoh was not just a political leader. In Egyptian culture, he was considered divine. Disobeying him could mean imprisonment, torture, or death.
These women had every reason to obey.
But they feared God more than they feared Pharaoh.
And that single decision changed history.
Because sometimes evil advances through the cooperation of ordinary people.
But sometimes it collapses when ordinary people quietly say:
“I will not do this.”

Shiphrah and Puah did not have armies.
They did not have influence.
They did not lead revolutions.
They simply refused to participate in evil.
And that kind of courage is one of the most powerful forces in the world.
Notice something else about this story.
Their act of faithfulness happened in private.

No crowds.
No applause.
No recognition.
Just quiet obedience inside the hidden rooms where babies were born.
But heaven was watching.
And God honored them.
The Bible says that because the midwives feared Him, God dealt well with them and established families for them (Exodus 1:20–21).
Their names were remembered.
Pharaoh’s command was not.
History rarely remembers the countless people who obey wicked orders.
But Scripture remembers those who feared God enough to resist them.
There is a deep lesson here for every generation.
Evil systems rarely function alone.
They rely on people beneath them to cooperate.

Sometimes that cooperation happens because of fear.
Sometimes because of pressure.
Sometimes because “everyone else is doing it.”
But the moment someone decides to obey God instead of man, the chain begins to break.
That is what these midwives did.
They stood at the fragile beginning of life and chose protection instead of destruction.
They chose obedience instead of fear.
They chose reverence instead of convenience.
And because of their courage, countless lives were preserved.
Including one life that would later change everything.
A Hebrew baby named Moses would survive Pharaoh’s oppression and grow up to lead Israel out of Egypt.
Imagine that.
Pharaoh tried to destroy a generation.
But two women quietly protected it.
This story reminds us of something incredibly important:
Faithfulness is not measured by how visible you are.
Some of the most powerful acts of obedience happen where no one else sees them.

In private decisions.
In moral crossroads.
In moments when doing what is right may cost you something.
The midwives show us that you don’t need a platform to be used by God.
You don’t need influence to stand for righteousness.
You simply need the courage to fear God more than you fear people.
Because the truth is this:
When the fear of man grows, compromise becomes easy.
But when the fear of God grows, courage becomes possible.
Shiphrah and Puah remind us that the Kingdom of God is often advanced not by famous heroes, but by quiet believers who refuse to help evil win.
Their story is a reminder that God sees what happens behind closed doors.
He sees the choices people make when pressure is high.
He sees the moments when someone chooses righteousness over safety.
And those moments matter more than we realize.
Because history is not only shaped by kings and rulers.
Sometimes it is shaped by two midwives who feared God more than Pharaoh.
And thousands of years later, their courage still speaks.
So here is the question this story leaves us with:

If you had been standing in that room…
With Pharaoh’s command hanging over your life…
Would you have obeyed the king?
Or feared God?
And maybe the deeper question for today is this:
Where in your life is God calling you to choose courage over compromise?
